procedural_history.impugned_order: Order made under section 3(1)(a) which the petitioner argued contravened article 22 (1) and (2) and was made in bad faith.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court decided against the petitioner on all points and dismissed the petition on 10-12-1954.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner appealed to the Supreme Court under article 32 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition.

issue.issue_text: whether s. 3(1)(b) of the Preventive Detention Act was ultra vires the Constitution inasmuch as it contravenes Arts. 14, 21 and 22 of the Constitution

law.name: Preventive Detention Act, s. 3(1)(b)
law.description: The section of the law being challenged as unconstitutional.

law.name: Constitution of India, Arts. 21 & 22
law.description: Guarantees the right to life and personal liberty and provides protections against arrest and detention.

law.name: Foreigners Act, 1946, s. 3(2)(c)
law.description: A related law upon which the challenged section is based, which also deals with foreigners.

application.reasoning: The Court determined that the Preventive Detention Act was a comprehensive law specifically framed with the constitutional limitations of Articles 21 and 22 in mind. It found that section 3(1)(b) was reasonably related to the Act's purpose. The power to expel a foreigner, granted by the Foreigners Act, necessarily includes the power to make arrangements for that expulsion, and using preventive detention is a valid method to prevent the foreigner from evading the expulsion order.

The Court held that the challenged section did not violate the right to equality under Article 14. It reasoned that the differentiation between different foreigners was based on a "reasonable and rational classification." The Court accepted that "reasons of State may make it desirable to classify foreigners into different groups" and found no evidence of individual discrimination.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge, holding that section 3(1)(b) of the Preventive Detention Act was intra vires (within the powers of the legislature) and did not violate Articles 14, 21, or 22 of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: whether, in any event, the detention was invalid as .it was made in bad faith.

facts: The petitioner argued that the government's real objective in detaining them was not for expulsion, but to hold them in custody until they could be handed over to West German authorities for extradition.

As evidence, the petitioner pointed to a letter from the West German Consul asking for their arrest pending extradition proceedings, and a subsequent note by a government Secretary suggesting the petitioner be kept in detention until a German boat arrived.
law: The Extradition Act gives the government discretion on whether to comply with an extradition request; it is not mandatory.
The government has the right to choose the less cumbersome procedure of the Foreigners Act when dealing with a foreigner, as long as the person leaves India as a free person.
application: The Court first noted that the initial order of detention was made *before* the West German Consul's letter was sent, so there was no connection between the two.
It found no material to suggest that the government changed its purpose for the detention after receiving the letter.
The Court dismissed the Secretary's note, stating it was merely a suggestion and could not be considered an order of the government or an indication of its official intent.
The Court also reasoned that because the government has the legal right to choose between the Extradition Act and the Foreigners Act, exercising this choice cannot be considered an act of bad faith.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, finding no force in it and concluding that the circumstances of the case did not show bad faith on the part of the government. Therefore, the detention was not invalid on this ground.

arguments.issue_text: whether s. 3(1)(b) of the Preventive Detention Act was ultra vires the Constitution inasmuch as it contravenes Arts. 14, 21 and 22 of the Constitution
appellant_arguments: Section 3(1)(b) of the Preventive Detention Act is not reasonably related to the purpose of the Act.
The arrangements for expulsion contemplated by section 3(1)(b) must follow and not precede the order of expulsion, especially as they involve curtailment of liberty.
respondent_arguments: Parliament's legislative competence to enact the law was not confined to just Entry 9 but could be based on other Entries as well.

arguments.issue_text: whether, in any event, the detention was invalid as .it was made in bad faith.
appellant_arguments: The detention was made in bad faith with the purpose of subjecting the petitioner to political persecution.

Once an extradition order is requested, a foreigner cannot be handed over to the government seeking extradition except under the Extradition Act, and the detention was a way to circumvent this process.
respondent_arguments: The question of bad faith regarding the expulsion was academic and should not be considered because no order of expulsion had yet been served on the petitioner.

cases.principle: The classification of foreigners is a reasonable and rational classification and therefore does not offend Article 14.
Only persons who are aggrieved by a piece of legislation can challenge it under Article 32 (the principle of standing).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The preventive detention of a foreigner by either the State or Central Government, with a view to making arrangements for their expulsion, is constitutionally valid. Such a law is within the legislative competence of Parliament and does not violate Article 14, as the classification of foreigners is permissible. Furthermore, it does not violate Articles 21 and 22, as the detention is conducted under a law that provides the 'procedure established by law' and falls within the constitutional exception for preventive detention.
obiter: The unrestricted power to confine and detain foreigners under the pre-constitution Foreigners Act, 1946, became invalid upon the passing of the Constitution because of Articles 21 and 22, which necessitated enacting provisions in the Preventive Detention Act to align the law with the Constitution.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The power to expel a foreigner, conferred by the Foreigners Act, implicitly includes the ancillary right to take effective measures to prevent a breach or evasion of the expulsion order. The Preventive Detention Act validly provides for detention as one of the methods of achieving this preventive end. Therefore, detaining a foreigner 'with a view to making arrangements' for their expulsion is a constitutionally permissible form of preventive detention and does not constitute bad faith, even when an extradition request exists, as the government has the discretion to choose the less cumbrous procedure.
legal_tests_applied: Reasonable and rational classification test for Art. 14
Doctrine of ancillary powers, where a primary power (expulsion) implies the necessary secondary powers (prevention of evasion) to make it effective.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that detention for expulsion is not 'preventive', reasoning that the right to expel includes the ancillary right to prevent a breach of the order, and the most effective method of prevention is detention.

The argument that arrangements for expulsion must follow an expulsion order was dismissed because the Preventive Detention Act expressly confers the right to detain 'with a view to making arrangements' upon both State and Central Governments, based on the satisfaction of either.

The claim of bad faith failed because the government has the legal discretion to choose the 'less cumbrous procedure of the Foreigners Act' over the Extradition Act. The existence of an extradition request does not fetter this discretion, and exercising a legal choice is not evidence of bad faith.

The challenge under Art. 14 was rejected on the basis that the differentiation between foreigners is based on a reasonable and rational classification, and reasons of State may make it desirable to classify foreigners into different groups.
why_respondent_won: The right to expel a foreigner under s. 3(2)(c) of the Foreigners Act implies ancillary rights, including the right to prevent any breach of the order and to take effective measures for that purpose.

The most effective method of preventing a breach of an expulsion order is by arresting and detaining the person; therefore, the right to make arrangements for expulsion includes the right to make arrangements for preventing any breach or evasion.

The Preventive Detention Act expressly confers the power to detain 'with a view to making arrangements' for expulsion upon both the State and Central Governments, and the 'satisfaction' required can be of either Government.

The government is given the right to choose between the procedures of the Extradition Act and the Foreigners Act, and no question of want of good faith can arise merely because it exercises the right of choice which the law confers.
policy_considerations: Reasons of State may make it desirable to classify foreigners into different groups.
The Government has the discretion to choose the less cumbrous procedure of the Foreigners Act when a foreigner is concerned, provided the person leaves India a free man.
